routes.title: The Mordell conjecture after Lawrence and Venkatesh, Part II: the Shafarevich conjecture for hypersurfaces in abelian varieties
routes.brief: Extend The Mordell conjecture after Lawrence and Venkatesh (MordellLawrenceVenkatesh) to the setting needed for the Shafarevich conjecture for hypersurfaces in abelian varieties, following Lawrence and Sawin, Annals of Mathematics 202 (2025), no. 3. It starts where that roadmap stops: there the method is run on the primitive cohomology of an abelian-by-finite family over a curve, with connected monodromy group and constant coefficients; here it must be run on the cohomology of a family with coefficients in a rank-one local system, with a possibly disconnected reductive group, and with a monodromy group known only to be strongly c-balanced. The final theorems are these. (1) Non-density (Theorem 8.17): for X a variety over ℚ with smooth model X over ℤ[1/S], E a constant H⁰-algebra, H one of GL_N, GSp_N, GO_N, and V a polarized integral E-module with H-structure, integral Frobenius eigenvalues and uniform Hodge numbers h^a with maximal torus of dimension t, if the differential Galois group G_mon ⊆ G⁰_dR is strongly c-balanced with respect to Frobenius and Σ_{a>0}h^a ≥ (dim X + dim H)/c and Σ_{a>0}a h^a > T((dim X + dim H)/c) + T((h⁰−t)/2 + (dim X + dim H)/c), then the image of X(ℤ[1/S]) is not Zariski dense in X. (2) The p-adic Bakker–Tsimerman theorem (Theorem 6.4): for a polarized integral Hodge–Deligne system with differential Galois group G_mon and period map Φ_p : Ω → G_mon/P on a residue disk, and Z closed of codimension at least dim X, the set Φ_p^{−1}(Z) is not Zariski dense. (3) Faltings's finiteness lemma for representations valued in a possibly disconnected reductive group (Lemma 5.49). (4) The main Diophantine theorems: for A an abelian variety over a number field K with good reduction outside S and ϕ an ample class in NS(A), there are finitely many smooth hypersurfaces H ⊆ A representing ϕ with good reduction outside S, up to translation, when dim A ≥ 4; when dim A = 3 and ϕ·ϕ·ϕ is not divisible by d(i) = C(a(i)+a(i+1), a(i)) for any i ≥ 2, with a(1) = 1, a(2) = 5, a(i+2) = 4a(i+1)+1−a(i); and when dim A = 2, from the Shafarevich conjecture for curves. Cover, in layers: Hodge–Deligne systems with their four realizations and four comparisons, their integral, polarized and integral-Frobenius variants, their Tannakian category and their differential Galois group; H⁰-algebras and their modules, with the GL_N, GSp_N and GO_N structures and the semilinearity of Frobenius that bounds its centralizer; the construction of E_I and V_I from a Galois orbit of characters; disconnected reductive groups — parabolic and Levi subgroups through cocharacters, G-complete reducibility, semisimplification, objects with G-structure, G-filtrations and the extension of D_cris to G-valued crystalline representations with its inner forms; adjoint Hodge numbers, the function T and uniformity; the p-adic period map on a residue disk and its image in a single orbit; index classes and the c-balanced and strongly c-balanced conditions; the semisimple case in full (Lemmas 7.1, 7.2 and Theorem 7.3) before the general case; purity forcing the average Hodge weight, balanced and semibalanced filtrations, bifiltered φ-modules and semisimplicity types, the finite list of types attached to a semisimplification, and the codimension estimates that make the locus of admissible filtrations small; and finally the assembly over the Weil restriction of the Hilbert scheme, with a resolution of singularities of an irreducible component of the Zariski closure of the integral points. Import, never re-plan: Faltings's finiteness lemma, friendly places and purity of Hodge weights from MordellLawrenceVenkatesh LV.1; the crystalline comparison on residue disks and the finiteness criterion from LV.4; the complex and p-adic period maps from LV.3; the abelian-by-finite families and Gauss–Manin transport from LV.2. Import perverse sheaves from EtaleDualityAndPerverseSheaves EDC.5, Tannakian formalism from MotivesAndAlgebraicCycles MC.6 and the Tau Ceti roadmap Reductive algebraic groups, Hodge structures from the Tau Ceti roadmap Hodge structures, period rings and crystalline comparison from PadicHodgeTheory R06.1 and CohomologyComparisons CP.2, weights and purity from WeilConjectures WC.3 and DeligneWeightsAndPurity DWP.7, abelian varieties and their Néron–Severi groups from AbelianSchemesAndArithmeticModuli A2, Riemann–Roch from SchemeAndStackFoundations SF.5, resolution of singularities from AlgebraicModuliForArithmeticGeometry R09.7, o-minimality and Ax–Schanuel from LogicAndDefinabilityInNumberTheory LD.6, and the big-monodromy input — the convolution monodromy group of a hypersurface and Corollary 4.10 — from the new roadmap proposed alongside this route, Sheaf convolution on abelian varieties and convolution monodromy (SheafConvolutionOnAbelianVarieties). Record that the Shafarevich conjecture for hypersurfaces is logically independent of Faltings's two finiteness theorems, and do not claim otherwise.
routes.reason: MordellLawrenceVenkatesh plans the Lawrence–Venkatesh method itself: Faltings's finiteness lemma, abelian-by-finite families, the complex and p-adic period maps, the crystalline comparison on residue disks and the assembly for curves. This paper needs new layers in exactly that direction and no other: the same three-realization argument run with coefficients in a rank-one local system, with Galois representations valued in a disconnected reductive group, and with a monodromy group known only to be strongly c-balanced rather than identified. The new material — Hodge–Deligne systems, H⁰-algebras and the semilinearity of Frobenius, complete reducibility and semisimplification for disconnected groups, D_cris for G-valued crystalline representations, adjoint Hodge numbers and the function T, the p-adic Bakker–Tsimerman theorem, the semisimplicity-type formalism and Theorem 8.17 — starts where LV.1–LV.11 stop and imports them. A new roadmap was rejected because every layer here is a strengthening of a layer there, and a source route was rejected because the generalizations are not statements those layers plan.

routes.title: Sheaf convolution on abelian varieties and convolution monodromy
routes.brief: Plan the Tannakian theory of sheaf convolution on abelian varieties and the convolution monodromy group, following Krämer and Weissauer and the first half of Lawrence and Sawin, Annals of Mathematics 202 (2025), no. 3, §§2–4 and Appendices B–C. The final theorems are these. (1) The convolution category: for an abelian variety A over a field, convolution makes the bounded constructible derived category a rigid symmetric monoidal category; perverse sheaves have non-negative Euler characteristic; those with zero Euler characteristic, the negligible ones, form a thick subcategory N; convolution of perverse sheaves is perverse modulo negligible sheaves; and P/N is a rigid symmetric monoidal abelian category which, after restricting to a character-dependent subcategory P^χ and to geometrically semisimple objects, is Tannakian with fibre functor K ↦ H⁰(A_k‾, K ⊗ L_χ). (2) The arithmetic–geometric exact sequence 1 → G_k‾ → G_k → Gal_k → 1 of Tannakian groups, and the fact that the Galois action on the fibre functor normalizes the commutator of the identity component of the geometric convolution monodromy group. (3) The convolution monodromy group of a smooth hypersurface (Theorem 3.5): for H ⊆ A smooth of dimension n−1, not a translate of itself by a nontrivial point, with n > 2 and outside two explicit exceptional cases, G_H contains SL_N, Sp_N or SO_N as a normal subgroup, where N = (−1)^{n−1}[H]^n; SL_N when H is not a translate of [−1]^*H, Sp_N when it is and n is even, SO_N when it is and n is odd. (4) Big monodromy from big convolution monodromy (Theorem 4.7 and Corollary 4.10): if the family of hypersurfaces over X is not a translate of a constant family, then for all characters outside a finite union of torsion translates of proper subtori, R^k f_*(g^*L_χ) vanishes for k ≠ n−1 and the geometric monodromy group of a c-fold sum contains (G^*)^c as a normal subgroup, uniformly over Galois conjugates. (5) Quasi-finiteness of the period map for hypersurfaces of a fixed class after pullback by multiplication by m (Proposition 4.11). Cover, in layers: convolution and its rigidity; negligible sheaves and the quotient category; character sheaves over k and over k‾ with their canonical descent; the Tannakian subcategories of geometrically semisimple objects and the two Tannakian groups; the Euler characteristics χ(A,L) = c₁(L)^n/n!, χ(H,O_H), the topological Euler characteristic and χ(H,Ω^i) = (−1)^{n−1−i}dA(n,i); minisculeness and simplicity of the distinguished representation through Krämer's characteristic-cycle criteria, with the modification needed when H is not invariant under inversion; the Hodge–Tate weights of the twisted cohomology; the elimination of the spin and exceptional cases and of the wedge-power case, including the Eulerian-number combinatorics of Appendices B and C and the sequence a(i) defined by a(1) = 1, a(2) = 5, a(i+2) = 4a(i+1)+1−a(i); the generic-vanishing lemma for characters outside a finite set of torsion translates of subtori; the battery of test representations detecting a power of a simple group; and the arithmetic avoidance lemmas that keep every Galois conjugate of the chosen character generic. Every definition gets its API and the concrete acceptance cases recorded in the extraction. Import, never re-plan: perverse sheaves, the perverse t-structure, intermediate extensions and Verdier duality from EtaleDualityAndPerverseSheaves EDC.1 and EDC.5; the Tannakian formalism from MotivesAndAlgebraicCycles MC.6 and the Tau Ceti roadmap Reductive algebraic groups; abelian varieties, their duals and ample classes from AbelianSchemesAndArithmeticModuli A2; Riemann–Roch and Chern classes from SchemeAndStackFoundations SF.5; Hodge structures from the Tau Ceti roadmap Hodge structures; weights and purity from DeligneWeightsAndPurity; and the Eulerian numbers with their elementary inequalities from ClassicalArithmeticCompletion CA.2. Export the big-monodromy statement to the Part II of the Lawrence–Venkatesh roadmap proposed alongside this route, which consumes Corollary 4.10 and nothing else from here.
routes.reason: Nothing in the atlas goes in this direction. EtaleDualityAndPerverseSheaves EDC.5 plans the perverse t-structure and intermediate extensions, but not convolution, not the quotient by negligible sheaves, not the resulting Tannakian category and not the convolution monodromy group; MotivesAndAlgebraicCycles MC.6 plans motivic Galois groups, a different Tannakian category; GeometricSatakeAndFusion plans convolution on affine Grassmannians, an unrelated geometry. The theory is a self-contained body of work of Krämer and Weissauer with its own applications — the Schottky problem and Katz's equidistribution theorems for character sums on abelian varieties — and this paper adds to it the computation of the convolution monodromy group of a smooth hypersurface and the transfer from convolution monodromy to ordinary monodromy. It is routed as a roadmap of its own so that the Part II of the Lawrence–Venkatesh roadmap can import a single big-monodromy statement, Corollary 4.10, rather than re-plan perverse-sheaf theory. The Eulerian-number combinatorics of Appendices B and C is kept here because it exists only to eliminate the exceptional Tannakian groups.

LD.6 plans o-minimal structures, definable counting and unlikely intersections, with Pila–Wilkie and Pila–Zannier as its named targets. The complex Bakker–Tsimerman theorem quoted as Lemma 6.3 — an algebraic subvariety of a period domain of codimension at least dim X meets the image of the period map only inside the preimage of a proper subvariety — is a theorem of that family, proved by o-minimal methods, and the paper states it in the exact form a Diophantine application needs. The atlas covers Mok–Pila–Tsimerman and Bakker–Klingler–Tsimerman but not Bakker–Tsimerman's Ax–Schanuel theorem for variations of Hodge structures, which is listed under prerequisites. The p-adic analogue the paper proves is not routed here: it belongs with the rest of the p-adic machinery in the Part II.

SF.0 owns schemes and morphisms with their named properties and is the most foundational layer that could own the Weil restriction of scalars along a finite étale extension, with its universal property and the resulting bijection on integral points. Neither library has it and no layer of the atlas mentions it, yet the main proof cannot start without it: Lemma 8.1 needs a base field with no CM subfield, so the whole argument is moved from K to ℚ by restriction of scalars. PROTOCOL.md section 15 asks that a general missing notion be planned once in its most foundational owner, which is this layer.

CA.2 plans sequences, recurrences, Bernoulli and Euler numbers, binomial identities and combinatorial number families. Eulerian numbers A(n,q), counting permutations by descents, with Σ_q A(n,q) = n!, the symmetry A(n,q) = A(n,n−1−q), the standard recursion and the elementary estimates (q+1)^n − (n+1)q^n ≤ A(n,q) ≤ (q+1)^n, A(n,q) ≤ n!, and the two sharper inequalities of Appendix C, are exactly that layer's subject. They are absent from both libraries: the occurrences of 'Eulerian' in Mathlib are Eulerian circuits in graphs. The paper is a good source for them because its appendices state and prove the inequalities in the form a consumer needs. The use of these numbers as the Hodge numbers of a twisted hypersurface stays with the new roadmap.
